Farm and woodland taxed at present-use value

Qualifying agricultural, horticultural and forest acreage may be taxed at its present-use value, a figure based on what the land produces rather than what a developer might pay. The classes are defined in G.S. 105-277.3, and the owner must ask for the treatment.

Present-use classes and their minimums
ClassAcreage in actual productionOther test
Agricultural10 acres; an aquatic species farm needs 5 acres or 20,000 pounds sold yearlyGross income averaging at least $1,000 over the three years before January 1
Horticultural5 acresThe same $1,000 average, with a separate minimum for Christmas tree land
Forestland20 acres outside any farm unitA written forest management plan

Ownership counts too. The land must be the owner's home site, or have been held by the owner or a relative for the four years before January 1, or have come from an entity or trust that already held the classification.

How to apply for present-use value

File the application with the assessor in the county where the land sits. G.S. 105-277.4 sets the windows.

  • First-time filers apply in the regular listing period, or within 30 days of a notice showing a changed value.
  • Later years need no new form unless the land is transferred or drops out through a change of use or acreage.
  • A buyer files within 60 days of the transfer date, and the form can go in any time in that calendar year.
  • Late forms need good cause, are approved by the county board, and help only for that calendar year's tax.

A disqualification notice must state the parcel number, the reason and the date of decision. The owner can appeal to the county board within 60 days, and after that the Property Tax Commission hears the case.

Selling land with deferred tax

The savings are deferred, not forgiven. The gap between present-use tax and full-value tax sits on the books as a lien against the land. A disqualifying event makes the deferred amounts for the preceding three fiscal years payable (G.S. 105-277.4(c)).

A buyer who wants to keep the classification has a path under subsection (b2) of G.S. 105-277.3. The land must have been at present-use value when title passed, and the buyer must keep the same use, file on time and certify acceptance of the deferred tax liability. Miss one of those and the deferred taxes fall due.

  • A conveyance to a government unit or qualifying nonprofit at or under present-use value wipes out the deferred lien.
  • A conveyance above present-use value makes a share due, set by a fraction printed in the statute, with the sale price less present-use value on top and true value less present-use value below.
  • Land that leaves only because of enrollment in the federal Conservation Reserve Program owes nothing deferred.

Get the deferred balance from the assessor in writing before you list, then hand a copy to your closing attorney.

Showing that farmland is well managed

The statute asks for a sound management program and lists ways to show one (G.S. 105-277.3(f)). An owner needs to show only one factor.

  • Enrollment in and compliance with an approved farm management plan.
  • Compliance with a set of best management practices, or with a minimum gross income per acre.
  • Evidence of net income from the operation, or that farming is the operator's main income.
  • Certification from a recognized agricultural agency in the county.

Forestland instead needs a written sound forest management plan for producing and selling forest products. A farm operator who meets the tests keeps the classification even when the owner collects rent rather than farming personally. Land under a qualifying conservation easement can also stay classified without production or income tests, provided the owner received no more than 75 percent of the donated interest's market value.

Due dates and penalties

  • September 1: bill due. Face-value payment is allowed through January 5.
  • From January 6: interest of two percent applies, and from February 1 each month or part of a month adds three-fourths of one percent more (G.S. 105-360).
  • Postmark rule: a mailed payment counts on the day it was postmarked.
  • Early-payment discount: allowed only where the county or town adopted a schedule by resolution before May 1 and the Department of Revenue approved it.

Phone the tax office for the discount schedule, if any, and for the exact balance before you send money.

Who is billed if the house sells midyear?

Whoever held title on January 1 is listed and billed (G.S. 105-285). Close in March and the bill still arrives in the seller's name. Put the division in the contract, and have it appear on the settlement statement.

One exception covers land exempt on January 1, such as property bought from a government body before July 1. The buyer lists it as of the acquisition date, at its January 1 true value, and it is taxed for the fiscal year starting that July 1.

Assessors use market value, meaning the price a willing buyer and seller would settle on with no pressure on either (G.S. 105-283), and reappraisal happens at least every eighth year (G.S. 105-286). An older appraisal date can leave your notice out of step with recent sales.

Disputing a value and relief programs

Ask the county board of equalization and review for a hearing before it adjourns (G.S. 105-322). If the board rules against you, written notice to the Property Tax Commission must arrive within 30 days after the decision is mailed (G.S. 105-290). Bring comparable sales and repair estimates.

Relief for homeowners is requested from the county assessor on Form AV-9. You can use only one of the programs below.

  • Age 65 or disability: the greater of $25,000 or half the appraised value is excluded (G.S. 105-277.1).
  • Disabled veteran: the first $45,000 is excluded, with no age or income test (G.S. 105-277.1C).
  • Circuit breaker: tax is capped at a share of income and the excess is deferred (G.S. 105-277.1B). The previous three years of deferral come due on a transfer.

Recovering tax billed in error

If the cause is a clerical error, an illegal tax or a levy for an illegal purpose, send a written demand to the taxing unit's governing body (G.S. 105-381). A refund demand may follow payment by up to five years from the due date or six months from payment, whichever ends later.

The body has 90 days to answer. A refusal or silence opens a three-year window to sue the taxing unit, and a winning judgment carries 6 percent interest plus costs.

Selling with taxes owed

The lien stays with the parcel. It attaches as of the listing date and carries the penalties, interest and costs along with it (G.S. 105-355). If a county enforces it, the vehicle is a civil action resembling a mortgage foreclosure (G.S. 105-374), ending in an auction at the courthouse door.

Redemption is open until confirmation if the person pays the taxes, penalties, interest and costs. Ask the tax collector for a payoff figure, pass it to the closing attorney, and let the title company pay it out of your proceeds. A quick cash sale can help if a deadline is near, though the lien still has to be settled at the table.

Frequently asked questions

What does present-use value mean on a tax bill?

Qualifying farm, horticultural or forest land is valued on its current use. The owner applies with the county assessor, and the tax difference is carried as a deferred lien.

How much land must be in production to qualify?

Ten acres for agricultural land, five for horticultural land, and twenty for forestland. Aquatic farms follow a five-acre or 20,000-pound test, and the income test averages $1,000 over three years.

Do deferred taxes vanish when farmland is sold?

No. The deferred tax for the preceding three fiscal years is due after a disqualifying event. A buyer who continues the use and accepts the liability in a timely application can keep the classification.

When does interest start on an unpaid bill?

January 6. A bill paid through January 5 costs face value, then two percent applies until February 1 and three-fourths of one percent per month follows.

Who gets the bill when I sell midyear?

The county lists whoever owned the parcel on January 1. The contract and settlement statement can shift the cost, so check the balance with the tax office.

North Carolina offers a property tax exclusion for qualifying elderly or disabled homeowners.

What the homestead exclusion does

North Carolina takes part of a qualifying owner's home value off the tax rolls. For the elderly or disabled exclusion, the amount removed is the larger of two figures: a fixed $25,000, or one half of the county's appraised value of the residence.

The state runs three owner-relief programs, and one form covers them all. Form AV-9 goes to your county tax assessor, since the Department of Revenue does not take it. An owner can draw on only one program at a time, so pick the one that saves the most.

Who qualifies for the elderly or disabled exclusion?

Three things must be true on the January 1 before the tax year: you live in North Carolina, you are at least 65 or totally and permanently disabled, and your prior-year income was at or under the cap. The rule is in Chapter 105, section 277.1 of the General Statutes.

  • The 2026 form sets the income cap at $38,800, up from $37,900 for 2025. It follows the Social Security cost-of-living percentage.
  • Every kind of income counts, with one carve-out: gifts or inheritances that came from a spouse, parent, grandparent or descendant. Spouses who share a home combine their incomes.
  • A protected residence is the dwelling plus its lot up to one acre and related improvements. Houses, apartments in multi-family buildings and manufactured homes all fit.
  • The disability needs certification from a physician who practices in this state or from a government agency.
  • A couple gets the whole exclusion even if only one spouse meets the test.

Disabled veteran exclusion

This one takes $45,000 off the appraised figure, and the state's own form says it has no age or income limit. Its statute is section 277.1C.

The owner must live in North Carolina, hold an honorable or under-honorable-conditions discharge, and either draw benefits under 38 U.S.C. 2101 or hold a VA certification of permanent and total service-connected disability. An unmarried surviving spouse can claim it too. Begin with a county veteran service officer, who helps complete Form NCDVA-9. Then file it at the assessor's office.

Circuit breaker deferral

The circuit breaker caps the tax bill at a share of household income and postpones the rest. Owners at or under the cap pay no more than 4.0% of income. Owners above it but within 150% of it pay no more than 5.0%.

The 2026 form puts those two thresholds at $38,800 and $58,200. Applicants must be at least 65 or have a total and permanent disability, live in this state, and have owned and occupied the house as their permanent residence for five years. You file every year, not once.

The postponed tax becomes a lien. If something disqualifies the owner, such as a transfer, a death or a move out, the deferred taxes for the previous three fiscal years become payable.

Comparing the three programs

North Carolina owner-relief programs, 2026 figures
ProgramWhat it doesWho it is forIncome test
Elderly or disabled exclusionCuts the bigger of $25,000 and half the appraisalAt least 65, or with a total and permanent disability$38,800 for 2026
Disabled veteran exclusionTakes $45,000 off the appraised figureQualifying disabled veteran or unmarried surviving spouseNone
Circuit breakerLimits tax to 4.0% or 5.0% of income and defers the excessAt least 65, or disabled, with five years in the homeUp to $58,200 for 2026

When and where to apply

The place to file Form AV-9 is the county tax assessor, and the time is the January listing window. It opens on the first working day of the year and closes January 31. Late applications are still taken through the first of June.

One form serves all three programs, so ask the assessor whether you meet more than one test. Each year brings a new income cap, so pick up the form for the tax year you are claiming.

What to bring to the assessor

Each county handles intake itself, so ask the assessor's office for its checklist before you go. Most files need the same evidence.

  • Proof of age, or the certificate of permanent and total disability.
  • Prior-year income records for the owner and for a spouse in the same home.
  • Proof the property is the owner's permanent residence, with acreage if the lot exceeds one acre.
  • For the circuit breaker, evidence of five years of ownership and occupancy.
  • For the veteran exclusion, the VA certification or benefits record and a completed Form NCDVA-9.

Arriving with every paper at the first visit saves a return trip and keeps you inside the January window. Make copies, and ask for a dated receipt when you hand the form in.

How the income cap changes each year

The state resets the number annually with the Social Security cost-of-living percentage. The 2026 form shows $38,800 against $37,900 for 2025, and its $58,200 upper circuit breaker line equals 150% of the 2026 cap.

An owner just over the line one year can land under it the next, so one denial does not decide later years. Circuit breaker relief ends unless you reapply annually. Ask the assessor whether your county wants repeat filings for the other two programs.

Can you also appeal the appraised value?

Yes, and the appraisal matters because every program here is measured against it. In most counties the commissioners act as the review board. Its first meeting comes in spring, somewhere between early April and early May.

Request a hearing, by letter or in person, before the board wraps up its work. A decision is mailed within 30 days after adjournment. An owner who still disagrees can give written notice to the Property Tax Commission within 30 days after that mailing. The elderly or disabled version takes the bigger of a flat figure and half the value, so a lower appraisal can change which side of that comparison controls. Call your assessor for the county's own appeal calendar and forms.

Selling a home that receives this relief

A sale is a transfer, and a transfer is one of the events that makes deferred circuit breaker tax payable. Get a written payoff figure from the county tax collector ahead of closing, so the title agent can pay it from your proceeds.

  • The seller also pays deed excise tax at the register's office before the deed is filed. The rate is one dollar for every five hundred of price, with any partial five hundred counted.
  • Each year's bill is due September 1, and anything unpaid picks up 2% interest on January 6.
  • Heirs who inherit from a circuit breaker owner may face the deferred bill too, because the owner's death is a triggering event.

Deferred tax is a lien, so clear it with the collector rather than leaving the buyer to find it. If you already receive any of the three benefits, tell your closing agent at the outset so the payoff request reaches the county early. A cash sale with a flexible closing date gives you time to sort out the payoff without a lender's deadline pressing on you.

Frequently asked questions

How large is the North Carolina homestead exclusion?

The elderly or disabled version cuts the bigger of $25,000 and half the appraisal. The disabled veteran version removes a flat $45,000.

What is the 2026 income limit?

It is $38,800 for 2026. For 2025 the limit was $37,900.

Where do I file the application?

File with your county tax assessor on Form AV-9. A disabled veteran first completes Form NCDVA-9 with a county veteran service officer.

Can I get more than one program?

No. The three programs are alternatives, and an owner draws on one of them.

What if I miss the January 31 filing date?

You still have time. Assessors must accept applications until June 1 of the tax year.

What North Carolina calls eviction

North Carolina calls it summary ejectment. The landlord files a complaint, the clerk of superior court issues a summons, and a magistrate in small claims court hears the case. Possession is enforced by the sheriff, not by the landlord.

The grounds are in G.S. 42-26: a tenant who holds over after the term, a tenant who breaches a lease condition that ends the estate, or a tenant who deserts the premises while in arrears. The process is built to be fast, and each step has a short deadline.

If you own a rented house and want to sell it, the steps below show how long a vacant house can take to deliver, and which steps you can skip by working out a move date with the tenant.

From filing to possession

A case moves in five steps: notice, complaint, hearing, judgment and writ. The timing at each stage is set by statute and court practice.

Summary ejectment steps and timing
StepTiming and rule
SummonsClerk sets an appearance date no more than seven days after issuance, weekends and legal holidays excluded (G.S. 42-28)
HearingSmall claims dates are set within 30 days of filing, usually within 10 to 15 days for evictions
Short serviceContinuance is mandatory if the defendant was served fewer than two days before court
JudgmentMagistrate orders possession if the plaintiff proves the case, the defendant admits it, or the defendant does not appear (G.S. 42-30)
AppealNotice of appeal to district court within 10 days of the magistrate's decision
WritSheriff must execute within five days of receiving the writ (G.S. 42-36.2)

The statutes behind these steps are G.S. 42-28, G.S. 42-30 and G.S. 42-36.2. The small claims page of the court system covers hearings and appeals.

Cost of filing a summary ejectment case

The small claims filing fee is $96 and the sheriff service fee is $30. There is no jury trial in small claims, which keeps the hearing short. Confirm both figures with the clerk before you file.

The landlord can also claim rent in arrears and damages for occupation after the lease ended, up to the small claims limit in G.S. 7A-210(1). A landlord who leaves those claims out of the summons case does not lose them in another action.

G.S. 42-46 controls what a landlord can add to the bill. It lets a landlord recover court filing fees, service costs and reasonable attorney fees under a written lease, with a cap of fifteen percent of the amount owed. It also permits one administrative fee per case, and only if the lease allows it.

  • A complaint-filing fee, if the tenant cures and the landlord dismisses before judgment.
  • A court-appearance fee of ten percent of the monthly rent, if the landlord wins in small claims.
  • A second-trial fee of up to twelve percent of the monthly rent after a tenant's appeal.

If the tenant appeals

A tenant who loses can give notice of appeal to district court, orally in court or in writing within 10 days of the magistrate's decision. Appeal costs must be paid and a bond may be required to stop enforcement.

That bond matters to a landlord who is also a seller. If the tenant appeals and posts what the court requires, the writ can be held up and a buyer may have to wait. Ask the buyer for a closing date that leaves room for the appeal window.

If the tenant does not appeal, the landlord asks for the writ. Before removing belongings, the sheriff gives notice of the approximate time. That notice is delivered to the tenant or left at the home at least two days before the stated time, or mailed first class at least five days before.

The tenant's belongings after a writ

Within seven days after the landlord is placed in lawful possession, the tenant may ask for property back, and the landlord must release it during regular business hours or at an agreed time. During that period a landlord may move items for storage but may not throw away or sell them, under G.S. 42-36.2.

After seven days, if the landlord offered to release the property and the tenant did not retrieve it, the landlord may dispose of it as G.S. 42-25.9(g) allows. If the sheriff stores the property, the sheriff can require the landlord to advance the cost of delivery and one month of storage.

  • Do not clear out belongings before the writ is executed.
  • Offer release in writing and keep a copy.
  • Photograph the house when you receive possession.

A buyer who wants the house empty will ask when it is clear and how the contents were handled, so keep your records handy.

Can I sell a rented house during an eviction?

A pending case changes what you can promise a buyer, because the delivery date depends on the hearing, any appeal and the sheriff. Ask your attorney how the contract should treat the case and who keeps the claim for back rent.

If the house is headed for foreclosure instead, the tenant's position differs. Under G.S. 45-21.16A, the notice of sale for a residential property with fewer than 15 rental units must say an order for possession may issue. A tenant under a rental agreement entered or renewed on or after October 1, 2007 may end the lease on at least 10 and no more than 90 days' notice after the sale date.

In a foreclosure the hearing takes place before the clerk of superior court, and notice of the hearing must be served at least 10 days ahead. A tenant who gets a foreclosure notice should read it closely and ask an attorney about the dates.

Where a landlord should start

Match the tenancy to the right notice and ground, gather the lease and payment records, and file with the clerk in the county where the house is. Then ask for the hearing date and plan the sale around it.

  • Confirm the notice period on our eviction notice page.
  • Collect the lease, the rent ledger and proof of delivery for any demand.
  • Ask the clerk of superior court for the current forms and fees.
  • Speak with a landlord-tenant attorney before filing if the lease is unusual.

When the tenant is willing to leave on a set date, a written move-out agreement can save the filing fee and the wait for a writ. Keep it in plain terms and have an attorney review it.

Frequently asked questions

What is summary ejectment in North Carolina?

It is the court action a landlord files to recover possession of rental property. The clerk issues a summons and a magistrate hears the case in small claims court, based on grounds in G.S. 42-26.

How fast is a North Carolina eviction hearing?

The summons sets a date no more than seven days after issuance, and eviction hearings are usually held within 10 to 15 days of filing. Small claims dates are set within 30 days at the outside.

How long does a tenant have to appeal?

Ten days after the magistrate's decision, orally in court or in writing. Appeal costs must be paid and a bond may be required to stop enforcement.

Does a tenant get a jury trial in an eviction case?

No. There is no jury trial in small claims.

Can the landlord keep the tenant's belongings after the writ?

Not at first. Within seven days of taking lawful possession the landlord must release property on request. After that, if the tenant did not retrieve it, G.S. 42-25.9(g) governs disposal.

Who can draft a quitclaim deed

Only an attorney admitted in North Carolina. G.S. 84-2.1 defines practicing law to include preparing deeds for another person, paid or not, so a friend, a broker or a form website cannot draft one for you.

The one exception in that statute covers real estate brokers acting as agents, who may choose or fill in a preprinted form under Real Estate Commission rules, and it covers preprinted residential leases. The same subsection then adds a flat limit: no non-attorney, and no website provider, may prepare a contract or deed conveying an interest in property located in the state, or pass on a title.

An owner who wants to sign a house over to a relative should start with a call to an attorney, not a template download.

What a quitclaim deed transfers

It passes along whatever interest the signer holds, if any, with no promise that the interest exists. The General Statutes use the word for releases of this sort. Under G.S. 52-10, spouses may release and quitclaim the rights each might gain through marriage in the other's property.

A release between spouses has a formality when real estate is involved. During the marriage, a contract or release touches neither spouse's real property unless it is in writing and both parties acknowledge it before a certifying officer. A notary public qualifies, along with court officials, and the officer cannot be a party to the contract.

Ask the closing attorney whether a quitclaim form or a deed with warranties suits your transaction, since buyers and lenders often want to see more than a bare release.

Quitclaiming a house between spouses

This works for property the grantor owns alone, and the receiving spouse takes it. The grantor's own spouse need not join the deed (G.S. 39-13.3). Some marital claims stay alive, however.

  • An elective life estate right survives unless the deed expressly waives it under G.S. 29-30(a)(2a).
  • A claim to equitable distribution under G.S. 50-20 cannot be waived or released in the deed at all.
  • Who keeps the house in a separation is a matter for a written agreement or a court order, which a family law attorney can draft.

Before one spouse comes off the title, read the loan papers and ask the lender how a change in title affects the mortgage.

Is excise tax owed on a quitclaim deed?

Only if the transfer involves value. G.S. 105-228.30 charges one dollar per $500 of consideration or value, rounded up for a fraction, and the transferor pays it before the register will record.

The article sets aside a list of transfers. Those include gifts, transfers by will or intestacy, transfers by operation of law, and any case where the transferee owes no money or property (G.S. 105-228.29). A family transfer with no payment usually belongs there. When a payoff or cash is part of the deal, let the closing attorney decide whether tax is due.

How common quitclaim situations are treated
SituationTreatment
Gift to a relativeOutside the excise tax
Transfer with money or property paid$1.00 per $500 of value, paid by the transferor
Spouse to spouse, grantor sole ownerVests in the grantee; the grantor's spouse need not join
Release of marital property rightsWritten and acknowledged by both spouses to reach real property

What the register checks at recording

The register looks at form and acknowledgment. Under G.S. 47-14, an instrument needing acknowledgment is accepted only when it appears to have been proved or acknowledged before an officer with apparent authority, with the officer's signature, commission expiration date and seal shown. The office is not required to rule on the sufficiency of the document or on the officer's authority.

Paper deeds also have to meet the layout rules in G.S. 161-14: letter or legal size, a three-inch blank top margin on page one, legible black print on one side, and the instrument type at the top. A deed that misses them can still be recorded for an added nonstandard charge.

This check says nothing about whether the grantor actually owned what the deed describes, which is why a title review matters.

Who can take the acknowledgment?

Any officer with apparent authority to take acknowledgments will do, and a notary public is the usual choice. For releases between spouses, G.S. 52-10(b) lists the certifying officers: a notary public, or a justice, judge, magistrate, clerk, assistant clerk or deputy clerk of the General Court of Justice, or the equivalent officers of the state, territory or foreign country where the acknowledgment is made.

The officer cannot be a party to the contract. For a spousal release signed outside North Carolina, the equivalent officer of the place where it is acknowledged qualifies. On any deed, the register looks for the officer's signature, commission expiration date and seal on the page.

Recording a corrected deed again

A corrected deed can be recorded again if page one is conspicuously marked as a rerecording. Under G.S. 47-14(a), the register may accept a previously recorded instrument or a certified copy marked that way, and the office does not recheck the acknowledgment or look for edits made after the first recording. An attorney should check the corrected text before it is resubmitted.

Why record the deed right away?

Registration is what makes a deed effective against outsiders. A conveyance is not valid against lien creditors or purchasers for value until it is registered in the county that holds the land, and priority runs by the time of registration (G.S. 47-18).

Suppose the grantor signs a second deed, or a creditor records a lien, before yours is filed. The later party may come out ahead. For land lying in two counties, the excise tax goes to the county with the greater value, so ask that office where to file.

  • Take the signed original with its notary page.
  • Bring the fee for the filing and, where it applies, the excise tax.
  • Keep the stamped copy with the book, page and recording time.

Checklist before you sign

Confirm who the record owner is and who has to sign. Then settle what happens to any existing loan and unpaid tax.

  • Ask the closing attorney whether the transfer counts as a gift or involves payment.
  • Ask the county tax office for the owner of record and any balance on the bill.
  • Look at how the current deed vests title, including any spouse's interest.
  • If a sale is planned soon, tell the buyer's attorney about the new deed so the title search picks it up.

A quitclaim deed gives a buyer or lender little comfort, so a sale of the house usually calls for a different deed. Sellers who want a plain cash closing can ask the buyer's side what deed and title work they will require before anything is signed.

Frequently asked questions

Is a do-it-yourself quitclaim deed legal in North Carolina?

Not when you prepare it for someone else. Drafting deeds counts as practicing law, and non-attorneys and website providers may not prepare a deed for North Carolina land. Call an attorney.

Will a deed to my child trigger excise tax?

Probably not, if it is a gift or nothing is paid. The statute sets gifts and no-payment transfers outside the tax, but any payment in the deal can change the answer.

Can a quitclaim deed end my spouse's equitable distribution claim?

No. A claim to equitable distribution cannot be waived or released in the deed. The elective life estate also survives unless the deed expressly waives it.

What happens if a quitclaim deed is never recorded?

It stays a signed paper without protection against lien creditors and purchasers for value. Later recorded interests in the same county can take priority.

What do I pay to file the deed?

A recording fee set by the fee statute, plus excise tax when the transfer is taxable. Ask the register of deeds in the county for the page count and the total.

What a North Carolina seller pays at closing

Expect four recurring costs on the seller side: deed excise tax, loan payoff, attorney fees, and filing charges for any paper you must record. Your total turns on the contract, so go through the attorney's settlement statement one line at a time.

Some charges are set by statute and others are bargained over in the sales contract. We stick here to the ones the General Statutes spell out, since they stay the same from one closing to the next.

  • The deed excise tax, which falls on the seller by law.
  • Paying off the mortgage or deed of trust, and getting that lien cleared from the record.
  • The closing attorney's fee for the deed and title review.
  • Register of deeds charges for any document you must record.
  • The year's county property tax bill, which runs on its own due date and interest schedule.

Agent commission, repair credits and the like come from your contract rather than the statutes. Get each of them in writing from the listing agent or the attorney before you sign.

Why a home sale needs an attorney

Under G.S. 84-2.1, drafting a deed or passing upon a title is legal work, so a lawyer has to do it. The definition names deeds, mortgages and title abstracting.

Brokers may fill in a preprinted form under that statute, and anyone may complete a preprinted residential lease, but nobody without a law license may prepare a contract or deed conveying North Carolina real property for someone else. So closings here happen at law offices.

Pick the closing lawyer early, or at least approve who does the work. This lawyer checks the title history, collects the payoff number, writes the deed, and makes sure the deed tax and filing charge get to the county. If a cash buyer chooses the lawyer, you can still ask to see a draft settlement statement early.

The excise tax as a seller cost

The seller owes it. G.S. 105-228.30 sets a rate of $1 per $500 of price or value, rounding any remainder up, and the transferor must pay before the deed is filed.

Because it tracks the price, this is frequently the largest line item the statutes assign to a seller. Expect your lawyer to deduct it from what you net and send it in with the deed. A tract that crosses a county line goes to the county with the greater value.

See our excise tax page for exempt transfers and how the money is split.

Register of deeds recording fees

One schedule in G.S. 161-10 applies in every county. The register of deeds collects up front, and the statute says no other fees may be added.

Recording fees under G.S. 161-10
Document or serviceFee
Standard instrument, first 15 pages$26.00 plus $4.00 for each added page
Satisfaction or cancellation of a loan lienFree

Each extra instrument within one document$10.00

Your deed sits in the first row. The buyer's lender pays the separate, higher schedule for a mortgage or deed of trust, so that charge rarely shows up on a seller's statement.

Mortgage payoff and the recorded lien

When the loan is paid off, the lender has 30 days to submit a lien release. G.S. 45-36.9 starts that clock, and filing the release costs nothing.

If the lender misses that deadline, it is liable for your actual damages. You may also send a written demand by a trackable method. Should another 30 days go by after the lender receives it, the statute adds $1,000 plus reasonable attorney fees and costs. That right belongs to the landowner who made the demand and cannot be assigned.

Home equity lines and other future-advance loans need an extra step, because the creditor must also get a request to close the line. Ask the attorney to send that request along with the payoff letter, so the old lien does not stay on the record.

When a deed takes effect against others

A buyer whose deed is not yet registered in the county where the land sits has no protection against lien creditors or other purchasers. G.S. 47-18 extends that rule to contracts to convey, options, leases running longer than three years, and first-refusal rights.

Priority goes by the time of registration, which is why attorneys file the same day the money moves, tax paid first. Do not consider the sale done until you hold the recording confirmation.

  • Confirm who records the deed, and when.
  • Get the book and page, or document number, after it posts.
  • File the recorded release of your old loan with your closing papers.

Property taxes at closing

County bills are due September 1 of the fiscal year and carry no interest if paid before January 6. Later payment triggers G.S. 105-360 interest of two percent, then three-fourths of one percent each month starting February 1.

The tax lien exists before the bill is mailed. G.S. 105-355 puts it on the parcel as of the listing date under G.S. 105-285, penalties and interest included, so title searchers look at tax status first.

How the year's tax is shared is a contract question. Pull the bill and its payment status from the county tax office, then have your attorney explain the split before you trust a net-proceeds estimate.

Questions for your closing attorney

Ask for every deduction from your proceeds in writing, each with the reason for it. A single phone call before closing day heads off most surprises.

  • What price is the deed tax based on, and which county collects it?
  • What is the payoff amount, and who follows up on the lender's release?
  • Which filing charges are mine and which are the buyer's?
  • How does the contract split the property tax bill?
  • When will the deed be filed, and will you send the confirmation?

Bring a photo ID and your loan account number to the signing. Check that your name is spelled on the paperwork exactly as on your current deed, since a mismatch can stall things while the lawyer prepares a corrected one. Living elsewhere? Ask about signing early before a notary and where your proceeds will be wired.

Use the same checklist when you compare offers. Statutory items do not move with the buyer, so any gap between two offers traces back to contract terms.

Selling while the house is in foreclosure

Costs can shift, since a power-of-sale foreclosure leaves timing to the clerk of superior court and the upset bid process. Under G.S. 45-21.27, each upset bid must exceed the reported price or last bid by at least 5 percent and no less than $750, and the bidder posts a deposit of 5 percent, never below $750. Each new bid reopens a ten-day window.

A sale that closes before the foreclosure concludes removes that uncertainty, though the lender may have piled fees onto the payoff. Request an itemized statement in writing and pass it to the closing attorney immediately.

The seller, as transferor under G.S. 105-228.30. The closing lawyer typically deducts it from your proceeds.

Can I close without a lawyer in North Carolina?

Not realistically. Drafting a deed or reviewing title counts as practicing law under G.S. 84-2.1, with narrow room for a broker's preprinted form or a lease form.

What does filing my loan release cost?

It is free. G.S. 161-10 sets no fee for a satisfaction, and G.S. 45-36.9 gives the lender 30 days after payoff to file it.

What does the county charge to file a standard deed?

Under G.S. 161-10 the first 15 pages cost $26.00, and every page after that adds $4.00. A nonstandard document draws an added charge, so ask the office.

Who handles probate

In each county, the elected clerk of superior court acts as the probate judge. Clerks and their assistant clerks hear most estate matters. A superior court judge steps in only when someone challenges a will in a caveat proceeding.

The register of deeds is a separate office. It records deeds and collects the excise tax, but it does not open estates or issue letters. A family selling a late relative's house will deal with both: the clerk early on, the register at the end.

Is the house part of the probate estate?

Not always. Land and houses are generally not administered through the probate estate unless the will says otherwise or the house must be sold to pay the estate's debts.

State law still decides who holds title. Under G.S. 28A-15-2, title to a decedent's real property vests in the heirs at the moment of death. Property left by a valid probated will vests in the devisees, and that ownership relates back to the date of death. A personal representative can petition the clerk for permission to sell the real property to pay debts and other claims (G.S. 28A-17-1).

With no will, intestacy law names the heirs. A spouse and children share in many cases, and a spouse and parents share when there are no children. A decedent with children but no spouse passes property to the children and the descendants of any child who has died. If no spouse, child or descendant survives, assets generally pass in this order: parents, then siblings and their descendants, then grandparents, then aunts, uncles and their descendants. Property held with a right of survivorship, or with a living named beneficiary, moves outside the estate. That covers life insurance, retirement accounts, joint bank accounts and annuities. Because the rules differ by situation, ask the clerk of superior court in the decedent's county whether an estate should be opened before you sign a listing agreement.

Probate routes compared

Three ways to settle a North Carolina estate (G.S. 28A-25-1)
RouteWhen it fitsCost or limit
Full administrationEstates that need a court-appointed representativeClerk issues letters; filing fee quoted at $120
Summary administrationSurviving spouse is the sole heir or deviseeAvailable with or without a will
Collection by affidavitSmall estates of personal propertyUp to $20,000, or up to $30,000 for a sole-heir spouse, after 30 days

The courts also run an online guide-and-file service for year's allowance, summary administration and small estate administration. The clerk's office can tell you which forms apply.

The small estate affidavit

An heir, a creditor or a public administrator can collect a decedent's personal property by affidavit at least 30 days after death. Two conditions apply: the personal property, less liens, must not exceed $20,000, and no one may have petitioned for or been granted letters. A surviving spouse who is the sole heir may use the process for an estate that runs above $20,000 but no higher than $30,000 after the spousal allowance is subtracted.

The affidavit goes to the clerk of superior court in the county where the decedent lived, and it must describe each tract of real property the decedent owned. The process itself covers personal property such as bank accounts and vehicles. If the estate holds a house, ask the clerk how that tract is to be handled and whether the sale needs a representative with letters.

How to open a full estate with the clerk

Go to the clerk's office in the decedent's home county. Some clerks take walk-ins, and others want an appointment. Bring the original will if one exists, a certified death certificate, a completed application and preliminary inventory, and the $120 filing fee.

  • An executor named in the will has first priority to receive letters, followed by any named substitute.
  • Without a will, priority runs from the surviving spouse to anyone receiving property under the will, then anyone who would inherit without one, next of kin, creditors, and finally a person of good character living in the county.
  • Out-of-state executors generally post a bond, and administrators post one unless an exception applies.
  • An estate can be reopened later if newly found property turns up.

A person who lived outside North Carolina can have an estate opened in any North Carolina county where property was left.

The creditor claims window

The claims deadline must fall at least three months after the notice is first published or posted. Once letters issue, the personal representative runs the notice weekly for four straight weeks in a newspaper qualified to carry legal advertisements. If the county has none, the notice is posted where the statute allows.

Known creditors get a copy by personal delivery or first class mail within 75 days after letters are granted. The state's Division of Health Benefits is notified when the decedent received medical assistance. Ask your title agent how it treats the claims period before you set a closing date.

Taxes and costs when selling an inherited house

North Carolina repealed its estate tax for deaths from January 1, 2013 forward, so those estates owe none. The costs that remain are property tax and the sale itself.

  • County property tax is due each September 1, and interest starts accruing January 6.
  • The seller pays deed excise tax at recording: a dollar for each $500 of value, rounding any partial $500 up.
  • Recording a standard deed costs $26.00 for its first 15 pages, then $4.00 per added page.

When a representative signs the deed, ask the title company which estate documents it needs to see, and request certified copies of the letters from the clerk in advance. Heirs who would rather skip repairs and showings can sell to a cash buyer, which keeps the sale simple once the clerk has confirmed who may sign.

Which office to call first

Start with the clerk in the decedent's home county, because that office knows whether a will has been filed and whether an estate is already open. Wills become public records once filed, and anyone may view one or request a copy for a fee. The clerk can also confirm whether anyone has already applied for letters, which saves you from listing a house that nobody has authority to sell. State law does not require a formal reading of a will, so families can go straight to filing it with the clerk and applying for letters.

If no will turns up, contact clerks in other counties where the person once lived, since some people deposit a will for safekeeping with a clerk. After that, call the register of deeds where the house stands to learn how the deed is currently titled.

Frequently asked questions

Who is the probate judge in North Carolina?

The elected clerk of superior court in each county acts as the probate judge. A superior court judge hears a caveat proceeding when a will's validity is challenged.

What is the small estate affidavit limit?

It is $20,000 in personal property after liens for most estates. A surviving spouse who is the sole heir may use it up to $30,000, after any spousal allowance is subtracted.

What does it cost to open an estate?

The filing fee is $120. Bring the will, a certified death certificate and the application and inventory forms, which the clerk's office provides.

Does North Carolina have an estate tax?

No. The estate tax statutes were repealed effective January 1, 2013, for deaths from that date on.

Can the house be sold while the estate is open?

Possibly, but who can sign depends on the will and on the heirs. Title to real property vests in the heirs or devisees at death, and a representative can petition the clerk to sell for debts, so confirm the route with the clerk of superior court first.

What the deed excise tax is

It is a levy on each document that conveys an interest in North Carolina real estate. G.S. 105-228.30 sets it at a single dollar for every block of five hundred dollars in the consideration or value of what changes hands.

The statute rounds up. Each time the price crosses into a new block of five hundred, the charge steps up by another dollar, even if the new block is barely begun. For an ordinary sale the base is the price written in the contract.

Who pays, the buyer or the seller?

The seller does. The law calls the seller the transferor and makes that person responsible for paying the county recording office ahead of recording.

At a typical closing the attorney holds back the amount from sale proceeds and sends it along with the deed. A cash buyer or investor changes nothing here. A contract may ask the buyer to cover a closing item, but that is a bargain between the two parties, and the statute still names the transferor.

  • The timing is fixed: payment precedes recording.
  • The recipient is the office in the county where the land lies.
  • The charge follows the deed, whoever ends up as the buyer.

Our closing costs page shows where this tax sits among the other seller charges.

Where the money goes

The proceeds are shared equally between two recipients. The home county takes one share for its general fund. The second share, less refunds and an allowance, goes to the Department of Revenue every month, and the county may retain two percent of it.

That split explains why you pay locally and not in Raleigh. The county collects first and forwards the state portion later.

A parcel that straddles a county line is assigned to one county only: the one holding the larger share of its value. If your land crosses a line, ask the attorney which recording office will take the deed, because that office decides where the paperwork lands.

Exempt transfers

Eight categories escape the tax under G.S. 105-228.29. A normal home sale fits none of them, since a sale means money or property flowing to the seller.

Transfers exempt under G.S. 105-228.29
Transfer typeStatute subdivision
By operation of lawSubdivision (1)
Lease for a term of yearsSubdivision (2)
Under a willSubdivision (3)
By intestacySubdivision (4)
By giftSubdivision (5)
No money or property due from the transfereeSubdivision (6)
Merger, conversion or consolidationSubdivision (7)
Instrument securing a debtSubdivision (8)

Row eight is why a lender's security instrument escapes the tax that a sale deed carries.

Inherited property

A transfer that happens through a will or through intestacy is exempt, so the heirs owe nothing when title first passes to them.

The charge appears when they sell. A deed from the heirs to a buyer is a transfer for consideration, so the sellers owe it, and with several heirs the attorney pays it out of the combined proceeds.

The state has also dropped its own estate tax for anyone who died from January 1, 2013 onward, under the repeal of Article 1A of Chapter 105. The deed charge discussed here is a different tax and still applies to a sale of inherited land.

Does paying the tax also record the deed?

No. Payment is a gate that comes first, and the filing is a separate act with its own charge, which our closing costs page lists from G.S. 161-10.

The filing matters because of G.S. 47-18. Until a conveyance is registered, it gives way to lien creditors and paying purchasers, and priority runs by the sequence of registration.

  • Pay the levy first.
  • Have the deed registered where the land lies.
  • Keep the receipted copy with your sale papers.

Recording a satisfaction of a deed of trust carries no fee, so a mortgage payoff adds no filing charge. A lease longer than three years, an option and a right of first refusal follow the same registration rule, so mention any side agreement to the attorney early.

What to confirm before closing

Check three things: the amount the tax is computed from, the county that receives it, and the settlement statement line that shows it.

  • The contract price and any other value that counts as consideration.
  • The county whose office will take the deed.
  • Whether an exemption in G.S. 105-228.29 really applies, for example a gift where nothing comes back to you.
  • That the tax shows once on the seller side of the statement.

Call the county office to learn how it accepts deeds for recording. The rate is statewide, and the procedure is where counties can differ. Ask for the draft settlement statement a few days ahead of closing so any mismatch gets fixed before you sit down to sign.

Other tax bills that can come due at sale

The county property bill is the main one. Under G.S. 105-277.1B, a senior or permanently disabled homeowner who has lived in the house for years can see the annual bill limited to a share of income, 4.0 percent in the lower band and 5.0 percent in the upper one. Whatever exceeds that share is postponed and sits on the property as a lien.

A sale ends the arrangement, as do the owner's death or a move out of the home. Three fiscal years of postponed tax then come due. A seller who used this relief should request that number from the county tax office well ahead of closing, since it lands next to the deed levy in the seller's column.

The disabled veteran exclusion under G.S. 105-277.1C takes a fixed slice of appraised value, $45,000 in the statute, out of the tax base for a qualifying veteran or surviving spouse. Ask the county assessor how a sale affects that exclusion.

Does the deed tax apply to a contract for deed?

The statute taxes each instrument that conveys an interest in real property. A contract for deed under Chapter 47H is a different paper: the seller keeps title while the buyer makes five or more payments, and the contract covers one to four family dwellings priced at $5,000 or more.

Chapter 47H demands a signed, acknowledged writing, lets the buyer back out through the third business day, and requires the seller to file the contract itself or a short memorandum within five business days. Whether and when a deed tax is owed on such a deal depends on the instrument used, so have the attorney confirm the answer before anyone signs.

Frequently asked questions

What rate applies to a North Carolina deed?

One dollar per five hundred dollars of consideration or value, with any leftover fraction counted as a full block. The same rate applies in all counties under G.S. 105-228.30.

Does the buyer cover the deed tax?

By default no. The statute puts the duty on the transferor, though a sales contract may move the cost by agreement between the parties.

Can a gift of a house avoid the tax?

A true gift is exempt under G.S. 105-228.29. If the recipient pays money or gives property in return, the no-consideration exemption fails, so check with the closing attorney before you rely on it.

Which office takes the payment?

The county recording office where the property sits. For land in several counties, the county with the larger share of the value takes it.

Is there a state estate tax on top of the deed tax?

No. The estate tax sections in Chapter 105, Article 1A, were repealed for deaths on or after January 1, 2013, and the deed levy is separate.

Is there a separate state tax on home sale profit?

No. North Carolina has a single flat individual rate and nothing special for gains. Whatever part of a home-sale gain survives the federal rules is taxed with the rest of your income.

State taxable income starts from federal adjusted gross income. G.S. 105-153.5, titled "Modifications to adjusted gross income," lists the subtractions and add-backs North Carolina applies. The sections below cover the ones that matter to a seller.

The flat rate for a 2026 sale

The rate is 3.99% for taxable years after 2025 and 4.25% for taxable years beginning in 2025. Further rate changes could apply from 2027 on, depending on triggers written into Session Law 2023-134.

North Carolina flat individual income tax rate by tax year
Tax yearRate

A flat rate means the state has no ladder of brackets. The federal return does use brackets, which is where the next sections come in.

Keeping the gain on your main home

Federal law shelters up to $250,000 of gain from income, or $500,000 on a joint return, for a qualifying main home. Because the state return starts from the federal figure, a sheltered gain generally stays out of North Carolina income too.

Two timing tests apply within the five years that end on the closing date:

  • You owned the house for 24 months or more.
  • You lived in it as your home for 24 months or more.
  • On a joint return, one spouse may meet the ownership test, but both must meet the use test.
  • A different home whose gain you excluded in the previous two years generally disqualifies this sale.

The months can be split between periods. Military, foreign service and intelligence personnel on qualifying extended duty can stretch the look-back period by up to 10 years. IRS Publication 523 has the full rules.

What to report and who files in North Carolina

If the closing agent issues a Form 1099-S, the sale goes on your federal return even when all the gain is excludable, and it goes there whenever part of the gain cannot be excluded. Use Schedule D and Form 8949.

For the state return, the gross income floor for tax year 2025 depends on filing status:

  • Single: file if federal gross income exceeds $12,750.
  • Head of household: $19,125.
  • Married filing jointly: $25,500.
  • Qualifying surviving spouse: $25,500.

A seller who moved into or out of North Carolina during the year is a part-year resident and files Form D-400 with Schedule PN, which apportions income. If the buyer pays over several years, the installment method applies unless you elect out, and the exclusion remains available.

Sellers who live outside North Carolina

A nonresident who sells a North Carolina house owes state income tax on the gain. Gain recognized for federal purposes from real property in the state is subject to North Carolina income tax, so the seller must file a state return and pay on that portion of federal taxable income.

The buyer has a duty too. Any buyer of North Carolina real property from a nonresident individual, partnership, estate or trust must file Form NC-1099NRS with the Department of Revenue within 15 days after closing, and send the seller a copy. The report lists the seller, the property location, the closing date and the gross sales price, including associated tangible personal property.

Estimated tax may also come into play. A nonresident must make estimated payments when expecting to owe $1,000 or more and expecting withholding and credits to cover less than 90% of the current year's tax or 100% of the prior year's. North Carolina did not conform to the federal deferral for gains invested in a qualified Opportunity Fund, so those gains must be included in a nonresident seller's state tax.

How a taxable gain is taxed federally

Property held for more than a year produces long-term gain. For tax years beginning in 2025 the rate on most net capital gain is 15% or less for most individuals, while gain on property held a year or less is taxed as ordinary income.

Breakpoints for 2025:

  • Single filers: nothing owed on gain while taxable income stays at or under $48,350, then 15% up to $533,400.
  • Joint filers: the 0% zone ends at $96,700 and the 15% zone ends at $600,050.
  • Heads of household: 0% through $64,750, and 15% through $566,700.
  • Above each 15% ceiling, the excess is taxed at 20%.
  • Unrecaptured section 1250 gain on real property has a 25% maximum.

The net investment income tax can reach large investment incomes, and a sizable gain may require estimated payments. A loss on a personal residence is not deductible.

Inherited or rented houses

An heir's basis follows its own rules, described in IRS Publication 551. Holding-period exceptions for property acquired from a decedent are explained in Publication 544.

The state estate tax is gone. Session Laws 2013-316 repealed G.S. 105-32.1 through 105-32.8, effective for decedents who died on or after January 1, 2013. Since then, North Carolina taxes an inherited house only through income tax when the heir sells it and has gain to report.

A rental house faces the same two-year use test as any other. Unrecaptured section 1250 gain is capped at 25%, so a landlord should have a CPA run the numbers before signing a contract.

State adjustments that touch a home seller

G.S. 105-153.5 holds several rules that interact with a sale:

  • Standard deduction: $12,750 for single and married filing separately, $19,125 for head of household, $25,500 for married filing jointly or a surviving spouse.
  • Itemized housing costs: qualified-residence mortgage interest plus real estate taxes together may not exceed $20,000, and spouses share one cap.
  • Other itemized lines: medical and dental expenses, and charitable gifts.
  • Opportunity Fund gains: gain that federal law defers into a qualified fund is added back for state purposes, and a matching deduction follows later so the same income is not taxed twice.
  • Basis gaps: when state basis and federal basis differ, an adjustment is made in the year of the sale.

For 2014 through 2025, the statute also made owners add back mortgage debt forgiven on a principal residence that federal law excluded. A seller who completed a short sale or loan forgiveness in those years should ask a tax professional how that rule applied.

The deed excise tax is a separate bill

The excise tax is a seller-paid recording charge of $1.00 per $500.00 of value or part of $500.00, collected by the register of deeds ahead of recording. Income tax is figured later on your return.

Hold on to the closing statement all the same. Gain is the sale proceeds less adjusted basis, and basis usually starts as the owner's cost, so your preparer will want purchase papers and improvement receipts.

Frequently asked questions

Does a house sale get its own North Carolina tax rate?

No. Gain is taxed under the flat income tax, which is 3.99% for taxable years after 2025.

What portion of my profit is sheltered when I sell my main residence?

Up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 for joint filers, when ownership and residence each reach 24 months inside the last five years. A prior exclusion within two years can block it.

Must I report a sale when none of the gain is taxable?

Yes, if you were sent a Form 1099-S. The sale goes on the return even though the gain is fully excludable.

What was the North Carolina rate in 2025?

It was 4.25% for taxable years beginning in 2025. The rate is 3.99% for the years after.

Does North Carolina tax an inherited house at death?

No estate tax applies for deaths on or after January 1, 2013. An heir who later sells the house may still owe income tax on any gain.

Transfer on death deeds in North Carolina

North Carolina has no transfer on death deed. The wills chapter of the General Statutes, Chapter 31, ends with Article 11, and that article covers electronic storage of attested wills by an attorney, not deeds that pass land at death.

The idea has been proposed. Senate Bill 160 in the 2023 session would have added a new Article 11 to Chapter 31, the Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act, with sections numbered 31-65 through 31-82. Its last action was a referral to the Judiciary committee on February 27, 2023. A bill that stays in committee does not become law, and the 2025 session law that did add an Article 11 dealt with electronic wills.

Laws change, so ask a North Carolina attorney before relying on any deed that claims to pass a house at death without probate. A form copied from another state does not create that right here.

What the 2023 bill would have done

It would have let an owner name a beneficiary by recorded deed, with the land passing at death and no gift made during life. The main features show what North Carolina owners lack.

  • The deed stays revocable during the owner's life, even if the document says otherwise.
  • It is treated as nontestamentary, and the owner needs the same capacity required to make a will.
  • It must be recorded to be valid, and no consideration or delivery to the beneficiary is needed.
  • The beneficiary takes the land subject to liens and interests that exist at the owner's death.
  • Liability for statutory allowances and estate claims could reach the property if the probate estate fell short.

None of this is in force. For now, owners here rely on wills, trusts and joint ownership to avoid or shorten probate.

How real estate passes at death without that deed

It passes under a will or to heirs by intestacy, and probate is handled by the clerk of superior court where the owner lived. A duly probated will is what passes title to real and personal property under G.S. 31-39. That section also sets a deadline: the will must be probated or offered for probate within two years of death, or before the clerk approves the personal representative's final account if that is earlier, for it to bind lien creditors or buyers from the heirs.

Wills must follow Chapter 31. An adult of sound mind, 18 or older, may make one (G.S. 31-1). An attested will is signed by the maker and two competent witnesses. A holographic will is written entirely in the maker's own handwriting and signed. A will can also devise property to a trustee of a trust set up before death, as G.S. 31-47 describes. Anyone can leave the original with the clerk of superior court for safekeeping, and G.S. 31-11 keeps it private until the owner dies.

Land in a second county adds a step. Certified copies of the will and of the probate certificate must reach the clerk of that other county inside the same two-year window.

Alternatives compared

Each option trades speed against formality. The table summarizes what the statutes provide for each one.

RouteHow it worksStatute
Attested or holographic willValid only if it meets Chapter 31; probate is needed to pass titleG.S. 31-3.2 to 31-3.4, 31-39

Small estate affidavitIn an intestate estate, personal property up to $20,000, filed with the clerk 30 or more days after death, when no personal representative petition is pendingG.S. 28A-25-1

The small estate affidavit covers personal property. It cannot move a house, so do not count on it when real estate is the main asset.

What can go wrong when a house goes through probate

The biggest delay for a buyer is title that is not settled yet. A caveat challenging the will can be filed within three years after probate (G.S. 31-32), and while one is pending the clerk's order bars distributions to beneficiaries. A title company will ask whether one has been filed.

  • No personal representative yet: ask the clerk who holds authority to sign a deed for the estate.
  • Heirs disagree: ask the clerk and a title company which signatures the closing requires.
  • Liens and taxes: each recorded lien and any unpaid property tax needs a payoff figure.
  • Records in another county: a will probated elsewhere has to be filed where the land lies.

The state estate tax was repealed for deaths from January 1, 2013 forward, so no state estate return is part of the picture. Federal rules are a separate question for the estate's lawyer or accountant.

Recording the deed after an heir or estate signs

A deed from an estate or an heir goes to the register of deeds in the county where the parcel sits. G.S. 47-18 withholds protection from a conveyance against creditors and later buyers until it is registered, and ranks competing filings by the time each was registered.

Statewide fees under G.S. 161-10 start at $26 for a short deed, and the transferor owes the seller's deed tax of $1 per $500 under G.S. 105-228.30 before filing. The register's office can give you a fee sheet with page counts and any recent change.

Selling an inherited house quickly

A quick sale is possible once someone has authority to sign and the title is clear enough to close. Heirs who would rather skip repairs and showings can ask Cash Home Buyers for an as-is offer. First confirm with the clerk who serves as personal representative, then gather the will, the letters and any payoff statements for liens or property tax. Take those papers to the title company early, since it will want to see who may sign before it schedules a closing. A cash sale also skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, which removes one source of delay while the estate is still being sorted out.

Frequently asked questions

Is a transfer on death deed valid in North Carolina?

No North Carolina statute authorizes one. A 2023 Senate bill proposed it and was referred to committee on February 27, 2023, and Chapter 31 does not contain the proposed article. Ask a North Carolina attorney whether the law has changed.

How can I leave my house to one person and avoid probate?

North Carolina offers no recorded beneficiary deed. A will passes title after probate, and G.S. 31-47 lets a will leave property to the trustee of a trust created before death. A lawyer can explain which structure fits your family.

How long does a will have to be probated?

A will has to be probated or offered for probate within two years of death, or before the clerk approves the final account if that comes sooner, to be effective against lien creditors and buyers from the heirs. G.S. 31-39 sets that rule.

Does the small estate affidavit cover real estate?

No, it covers personal property of up to $20,000 in an intestate estate (more for a surviving spouse who is the sole heir) under G.S. 28A-25-1. The affidavit goes to the clerk of superior court in the county where the person lived, no sooner than 30 days after death.

Does North Carolina charge an estate tax?

No. G.S. 105-32.1 through 105-32.8 were repealed for estates of people who die on or after January 1, 2013. Federal estate rules are separate.

What to bring to the register of deeds

Bring a deed with a completed notary acknowledgment. G.S. 47-14 tells the register not to accept a paper that needs an acknowledgment unless the officer's signature, commission expiration date and any required seal appear on it.

  • The signed instrument with the notary page attached.
  • Letter-size or legal-size paper, with a blank band of three inches across the top of page one.
  • Black print on white stock at 9 points or larger, one side only.
  • The kind of instrument written at the head of the first page.
  • Payment for the recording charge and any excise tax.

Paper that fails these format points is still recorded, with the nonstandard add-on from G.S. 161-14. Where the only flaw is type smaller than 9 points, a register may waive the add-on if the text is readable.

How fast documents are recorded

Papers are registered strictly in arrival order, and each is endorsed with the day and hour it was handed in. The register records on the day of presentation unless a temporary index is running, and permanent indexing must still be done within 30 days (G.S. 161-14).

The stamp carries legal weight. Under G.S. 47-18, a lease running past three years, an option, a right of first refusal or a conveyance is ineffective against lien creditors and purchasers for value until registered, and the order of registration by time sets priority. A buyer therefore wants the deed recorded quickly.

Electronic recording and paper copies

Electronic recording is for approved submitters only. Subsection (a1) of G.S. 47-14 covers e-documents from a federal or state government body and from a trusted submitter, meaning one that signed an electronic recording agreement with that county's register. Ask the office whether your closing attorney is set up.

A paper fallback exists. The register must take a printout of an electronic document if the county has no e-recording, if its system rejects that document type, or if the system is down at the time. A sworn certificate must say the printout is accurate and unchanged. Telephone the office before you mail anything.

  • Learn which payment forms the office accepts.
  • Put the property address and a return address on a mailed deed.
  • Hold on to the receipt that shows book, page and time.

Recording a paper again

An already recorded paper can be recorded again as a rerecording. Mark page one of the earlier instrument, or of a certified copy, in plain view as a rerecording (G.S. 47-14(a)). This helps after a recording mistake has been fixed.

The register can rely on the marking and the old recording data without rechecking the acknowledgment or searching for later edits. A corrected deed deserves a lawyer's review before resubmission.

Seals get their own presumption. A record the register accepts is presumed to have borne a clear notary seal image, and the office cannot refuse a record on the ground that the seal misses the notary statute's standard. If a court later finds a seal invalid, anyone who recorded an interest ahead of that finding keeps it.

Which filings fall under the paper-format rules?

The format rules apply to filings that carry a fee under the fee statute. G.S. 161-14(d) names five groups.

  • Instruments in general, which is where a deed falls.
  • Deeds of trust, mortgages, and cancellations of both.
  • Uniform Commercial Code filings.
  • Torrens registrations.
  • Master forms.

Certified copies of court-filed documents and filings that follow the UCC filing-office rules are excused from the paper-size and margin rules.

When the register is a party to the document

A document in which the county's own register is a party can be proved or acknowledged before any magistrate or notary public (G.S. 47-14(e)). Home sales rarely raise this, but it is the one case where the statute names magistrates as acknowledging officers.

If the register turns your document away

A district court judge in the district can order registration. G.S. 47-14(b) gives this route to the person offering an instrument the register declined. The judge must find that the signer's execution was proved or acknowledged before an authorized officer, and that the officer's signature, commission expiration date and any required seal are present.

The register does not rule on legal sufficiency, so a recorded deed does not prove that it works. Ask an attorney to confirm title before you lean on the record. If you are selling, have the closing attorney or title company handle the filing so a rejected page does not delay the closing.

Frequently asked questions

Which county office takes a deed for my house?

The register of deeds where the house stands. For a parcel that crosses a county line, the office in the county with the greater value collects the excise tax and can say how to file.

What does a register of deeds charge for a standard deed?

Up to 15 pages cost $26.00 together, and extra pages are $4.00 each. Excise tax may be due as well, paid at the same counter.

Is there a charge for filing proof that a mortgage was paid?

No. The fee statute sets no charge for a satisfaction or cancellation of a deed of trust or mortgage.

Why would a register of deeds refuse a deed?

Usually because a required acknowledgment does not appear to have been taken before an officer with authority. A district court judge can order registration if the proof or acknowledgment meets the statute.

How soon after I hand in a deed does it appear in the index?

The register is meant to record it the same day. An office using a temporary index must still finish permanent indexing within 30 days after presentation.
